title: Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. v. M/s Galaxy Traders & Anr.
ratio_decidendi: The limitation period of 15 days for making payment under Section 138 proviso (c) begins only when the drawer receives the notice, not when the payee dispatches it. The cause of action to file a complaint arises only upon failure of the drawer to pay within 15 days of such receipt.
content: The Supreme Court held that Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was enacted to enhance the acceptability of cheques in settlement of liabilities by making the drawer liable for penalties in case of bouncing of cheques. The period of 15 days prescribed under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138 is to be computed from the date of the receipt of the notice by the drawer and not from the date of its dispatch. The cause of action for filing the complaint under Section 142 arises only on the day following the expiry of 15 days from the receipt of the notice.

title: Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v. State of Maharashtra
superseded_by: Overcome by Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2015 introducing Section 142(2)
legal_issues: Territorial jurisdiction in cheque bounce cases
Place of dishonour vs place of bank branch
ratio_decidendi: Territorial jurisdiction is restricted to the place where the drawee bank is situated. (Note: Subsequently, Parliament amended Section 142(2) in 2015 to clarify that jurisdiction lies where the payee delivers the cheque through their own bank account branch).
content: A three-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that the territorial jurisdiction for initiating criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is restricted only to the court within whose local jurisdiction the offence is committed, namely, where the cheque is dishonoured by the bank on which it is drawn. Parliament later enacted the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act 2015 inserting Section 142(2) to provide convenience to the payee.

title: Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons & Ors.
legal_issues: Validity of eviction notice under Section 106
ratio_decidendi: When a lease deed is unregistered despite exceeding one year, it cannot create a lease of longer duration, but creates a month-to-month tenancy terminable by 15 days notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
content: The Supreme Court examined the legal effect of an unregistered lease agreement for a period exceeding one year. The Court ruled that under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, a lease from year to year or exceeding one year must be registered. If unregistered, it cannot be received as evidence of a long-term lease. However, payment of rent creates a month-to-month tenancy by implication of law, which can be lawfully terminated by the landlord by issuing a valid 15-day notice to quit under Section 106.

title: Superintendence Company of India (P) Ltd. v. Krishan Murgai
ratio_decidendi: A restrictive covenant in an employment agreement that restrains an employee from carrying on a similar trade or working with a competitor after termination of employment is void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
content: The Supreme Court held that under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is to that extent void. While negative covenants applicable during the period of employment are generally valid to ensure dedication to the employer, any non-compete clause that seeks to restrain the employee post-termination is entirely void and unenforceable against the employee under Indian law.

title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Harsolia Motors
legal_issues: Deficiency in service in insurance claim repudiation
ratio_decidendi: A commercial entity taking an insurance policy to indemnify against accidental loss does not do so for 'commercial purpose' or profit-making, and is entitled to file a consumer complaint for deficiency in service upon wrongful claim repudiation.
content: The Supreme Court clarified the scope of 'commercial purpose' under the Consumer Protection framework. Taking an insurance policy is for indemnification of loss, not for direct profit generation or commercial activity. Therefore, commercial enterprises are fully entitled to approach the Consumer Commission under the Consumer Protection Act for arbitrary repudiation or deficiency in service by insurance providers.
